title: Seneca gets seasick
hook: Seneca gets so seasick he jumps overboard; our faults are hidden until we recover (Letters 53)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Harpaste, who blamed the house for her own dark. Your line was the dark is in me.

The sea looks calm. Seneca, who should know better, lets himself be talked into a short crossing of the bay near Naples, cutting straight over open water to save time. Once he's too far out for turning back to matter, the sky turns, the swell builds, and the great philosopher of calm becomes very, very sick. He begs the pilot to put him ashore. The pilot says there's nowhere to land. What happens next is not dignified, and Seneca tells it himself, on purpose.
screen: `A CALM SEA, A SHORT TRIP.` → `THE SWELL BUILDS.` → `THE PHILOSOPHER OF CALM, VERY SICK.`

segments.voice: The pilot won't steer for the rocky shore, so Seneca, an old devotee of cold water, as he calls himself, throws himself into the sea, swims for land and crawls up the rocks. Only then, he says, did he understand that seasickness doesn't leave you just because you've reached dry ground. A sick body sends signals, he notes: a heavy ache, a fever creeping in. You can't miss them for long. Faults of the mind are the opposite. The worse they are, the less we feel them. Someone lightly asleep notices their dreams, and sometimes knows they're dreaming. Someone in a deep sleep doesn't even know they're asleep. Why does nobody confess their faults? Because they're still in them. Telling your dream is for someone who's awake. So, Seneca says, admitting your faults is a sign of returning health: vitia sua confiteri sanitatis indicium est. The moment you can say, oh, that's what I do when I'm afraid, you're already climbing up the rocks. Noticing a fault, in Seneca's picture, is the fever starting to break.
screen: `SENECA JUMPS OVERBOARD.` · `THE BODY SENDS SIGNALS.` · `THE SOUL'S FAULTS HIDE.` · `ADMITTING IT IS HEALTH.` · then, large: `AWAKE TO IT.`

segments.voice: Notice one signal your body is sending right now, a tight jaw, tired eyes, an empty stomach; it didn't wait to be asked. Now bring to mind someone who knows you well, and ask what they might say you do when you're tired or rushed, the thing you never mention. Don't argue with the answer; hold it the way you'd hold a dream you've just woken from.
Confiteri. Latin for to confess: admitting your faults, Seneca says, is a sign of returning health. Today's word.
Your line: awake to it. Only someone awake can tell the dream. On to tomorrow.

howItsDone: Readers of Seneca often treat noticing a new fault as progress rather than failure, and some keep a brief note of faults they have recently become aware of.

chat.says: Why would Seneca tell such an embarrassing story about himself?
options: To show the soul's faults hide like deep sleep, and admitting them is a sign of health.
To show a real philosopher never gets sick or scared, even in a storm at sea.
To warn readers that boats are dangerous and land is always the safer road.
chat.meaning: Letter fifty-three: illness of the body announces itself, but faults of the mind hide like deep sleep. Confessing them means you're waking up.

notes: Letters 53.1–4: the voyage from Parthenope to Puteoli, the pilot's refusal, Seneca's leap ('vetus frigidae cultor'), climbing the rocks, and that nausea persisted on land. Confirm.

53.5–8: bodily illness signals vs hidden diseases of the soul, the light and deep sleep image, 'somnium narrare vigilantis est', 'vitia sua confiteri sanitatis indicium est'. Confirm wording and numbering.
Note: Seneca was in fact aged (he was in his sixties) when this happened; the script doesn't give his age.
